uncited: **Detect Case**: Determine the position of the ray origin $o$ relative to the bounding volume $B$ and the object $f$.
- Compute $t_b = \text{intersect\_ray\_convex}(o, d, B)$.
If `None`, the ray does not intersect the bounding volume; return `None`.
- Check if $o$ is inside the object: $inside\_obj = (f(o) < 0)$.
- Check if $o$ is inside the bounding volume: $inside\_bound = \text{point\_in\_convex}(o, B)$.
- **Case 1**: Origin outside bounding volume ($o \notin B$).
- **Case 2**: Origin inside bounding volume but outside object ($o \in B$ and $f(o) \ge 0$).
- **Case 3**: Origin inside bounding volume and inside object ($o \in B$ and $f(o) < 0$).
- The ray enters the bounding volume at $t_b$.
- The ray is already inside the bounding volume but outside the object.
Tracing forward through the interior is costly.
- Find the intersection of the ray with the bounding volume in the forward direction.
- Compute the point on the bounding volume boundary: $p_{bound} = o + t_b \cdot d$.
- Perform sphere tracing in the **inverse** ray direction starting from $p_{bound}$.
- Inverse ray: origin $p_{bound}$, direction $-d$.
- Trace using $f(p)$ until an intersection is found.
Let the distance along the inverse ray be $t_{inv}$.
- The intersection point in world space is $p_{hit} = p_{bound} - t_{inv} \cdot d$.
This is significantly faster for large objects.
The optimization was proposed by Hart et al. [Har96] for sphere tracing convex objects.
